Question B-007-005-007.

Why the correct answer is right: High sunspot numbers usually mean stronger ionization and a higher maximum usable frequency (MUF). Under those conditions, frequencies at the top of the high-frequency (HF) range and above, up to about 40 MHz or more, can support long-distance contacts.

Why the distractors are wrong:
- sourceIndex 1: "High frequency radio signals are absorbed": Absorption is mainly a lower-ionosphere problem on lower HF. High sunspot activity more often raises usable upper-HF frequencies.
- sourceIndex 2: "Frequencies up to 100 MHz or higher are normally usable for long-distance communication": One hundred megahertz is into the very high frequency (VHF) range, where long paths require special modes rather than normal HF solar-cycle improvement.
- sourceIndex 3: "High frequency radio signals become weak and distorted": Weak or distorted signals can happen on particular paths, but that is not the general propagation benefit of high sunspot numbers.
